identification.summary: Water Gamayun is Trend Micro's name for a Russian threat actor (per Trend Micro) also known as EncryptHub and Larva-208 [S1][S2]. Trend Micro reported it exploiting the Microsoft Management Console zero-day CVE-2025-26633 ('MSC EvilTwin'), patched 11 March 2025 [S1][S2]. Its delivery methods include provisioning packages (.ppkg), signed Windows Installer (.msi) files and .msc files [S2]. Its arsenal includes the EncryptHub Stealer, the SilentPrism and DarkWisp backdoors, Stealc and Rhadamanthys [S1][S2][S3]. Zscaler describes it as a Russia-aligned APT group [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro says EncryptHub gained attention toward the end of June 2024, when it pushed malware through a GitHub repository named 'encrypthub' tied to a fake WinRAR website [S2]. Prodaft likewise places the start of operations around June 2024 [S4].
identification.notes: Trend Micro (Water Gamayun), Prodaft (Larva-208) and the 'EncryptHub' persona are presented by the cited sources as the same activity [S2][S4]. Outpost24 reporting describes a likely lone individual behind the EncryptHub alias, which differs from the 'APT group' framing in Trend Micro and Zscaler titles [S5][S3]. Microsoft's threat actor naming taxonomy was not checked; no Microsoft name is asserted.

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered. Trend Micro identifies the actor as Russian and Zscaler calls it Russia-aligned [S1][S2][S3]. Outpost24 and Prodaft describe a financially motivated, ransomware-linked operation [S4][S5].
attribution.confidence: Trend Micro's page states the Russian attribution without a hedge [S2]. Zscaler attributed its observed campaign to Water Gamayun with high confidence, based on TTP overlap with public reporting (MSC EvilTwin use, obfuscation, window-hiding) [S3]. These are vendor assessments only; no government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Vendor assessment (Trend Micro, Zscaler) [S1][S3]. Outpost24 found an exposed configuration file on the actor's C2 server containing Telegram bot information, plus reused passwords and no 2FA, and reported the actor sold exploits on a Russian-language forum [S5].

objectives: Prodaft assesses the operation as social engineering with ransomware as the end goal, and says it may act as an initial access broker or direct affiliate for RansomHub and BlackSuit [S4]. Outpost24 describes the actor as financially motivated [S5].

targeting.notes: Sources describe opportunistic targeting of organizations and individuals rather than named sectors. Prodaft reports at least 618 compromised organizations [S4]. Trend Micro reports installers masquerading as DingTalk, QQTalk and VooV Meeting [S2]. Sector and regional distribution is not given in the gathered sources.

capabilities.summary: Exploitation of CVE-2025-26633 (MSC EvilTwin) via rogue .msc files and the MUIPath setting [S2]. Delivery through .ppkg, signed .msi and .msc files; the MSC EvilTwin loader leads to Rhadamanthys and cleans up forensic traces [S2]. The custom stealer collects Wi-Fi passwords, Windows product keys, clipboard history, browser credentials and application session data [S2]. Trend Micro documents living-off-the-land use of PowerShell run through the IntelliJ launcher runnerw.exe [S1]. Prodaft reports SMS and voice phishing posing as IT help desk, fake VPN login pages, remote monitoring tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer), real-time MFA and session-cookie capture, and a custom PowerShell encryptor [S4]. Prodaft reports about 70 purchased domains imitating Cisco, Palo Alto and Fortinet VPN products [S7]. Outpost24 reports the actor used ChatGPT for writing, translation and infrastructure help [S5].

campaigns.name: Fake WinRAR and GitHub malware distribution
campaigns.summary: EncryptHub first drew attention by distributing malware through a GitHub repository named 'encrypthub' and a fake WinRAR site, later moving to its own staging and C2 infrastructure [S2].

campaigns.name: Larva-208 social engineering and infostealer operations
campaigns.summary: Prodaft reports vishing and SMS phishing against at least 618 organizations, followed by infostealers (Stealc, Rhadamanthys) and in many cases ransomware, with links to RansomHub and BlackSuit [S4].

campaigns.name: Outpost24 exposure of EncryptHub
campaigns.summary: Outpost24 KrakenLabs (blog dated 6 March 2025) described OPSEC failures including an exposed C2 configuration file, reused passwords and ChatGPT use, and noted Microsoft credited the likely lone actor behind the alias with reporting CVE-2025-24061 and CVE-2025-24071 [S5].

campaigns.name: MSC EvilTwin (CVE-2025-26633) exploitation
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reported Water Gamayun exploiting the MMC zero-day, patched 11 March 2025, to deploy SilentPrism, DarkWisp, EncryptHub Stealer and Rhadamanthys; Trend Micro and Zero Day Initiative coordinated disclosure with Microsoft [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Zscaler-reconstructed Water Gamayun intrusion
campaigns.summary: Zscaler Threat Hunting described an attack chain from Bing search results to a compromised site and lookalike domain using the MSC EvilTwin flaw with encoded PowerShell; the final payload could not be confirmed because C2 was unresponsive [S3].

diamond.adversary: Suspected Russian actor; Outpost24 assesses a likely lone individual using the EncryptHub alias, while Prodaft links the activity to RansomHub and BlackSuit [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.capability: CVE-2025-26633 exploitation, .ppkg/.msi/.msc delivery, EncryptHub Stealer, SilentPrism, DarkWisp, Stealc, Rhadamanthys, PowerShell and runnerw.exe LOLBin use [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Initially a GitHub repository, later own staging and C2 servers [S2]; roughly 70 VPN-lookalike domains [S7]; Telegram bots [S5]; compromised sites and lookalike domains reached via Bing search results [S3].
diamond.victim: At least 618 organizations per Prodaft [S4]; users of messaging and meeting software lured by trojanized installers [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financially motivated, with ransomware affiliation reported [S4]. A Russian-language forum presence is reported [S5]. No state tasking is evidenced in the gathered sources.
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and MMC (CVE-2025-26633), PowerShell, user trust in help-desk calls, fake VPN portals and search-engine results; MFA relying on one-time codes or session cookies [S2][S3][S4].

gaps: Trend Micro's original two-part research and the Zscaler blog could not be fetched in this session (fetch failed); facts rely on search-result summaries of those documents and secondary coverage. Re-verify against the primary pages.
Exact publication dates for the Trend Micro, Hacker News and BleepingComputer articles were not confirmed; month-level dates are used.

The Prodaft primary report was not opened; its findings are taken from BleepingComputer and Anvilogic coverage [S4][S7]. The count of 618 organizations and the affiliate versus access-broker role differ across coverage.
Whether 'Water Gamayun' is a single individual or a group is unresolved: Outpost24 describes a likely lone actor, while Trend Micro and Zscaler use group framing [S3][S5].
No government attribution, sponsor, or Microsoft/MITRE name was verified; MITRE group ID is not assigned in the record.
Sector and regional victimology is not published in the gathered sources.
Status of the actor after the Outpost24 exposure and after Zscaler's November 2025 report is unknown.
A Hacker News article on Outpost24 research could not be confirmed in search results and was removed along with claims resting only on it (LabInstalls, Outpost24 lure list).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Endpoint and remote-access terrain is key: Windows workstations running MMC, VPN clients, and help-desk and remote-support workflows [S2][S4]. STEP 2: The actor is financially motivated and opportunistic with ransomware affiliations, not shown to be state-tasked [S4][S5]. STEP 3: The template is vishing or SMS phishing or trojanized installer or search-engine lure, then PowerShell and stealer or backdoor, then credential and VPN-session theft, then possible ransomware [S2][S3][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is credential and VPN-session theft against organizations and individuals, including DoD-adjacent contractors, via fake VPN and meeting apps, feeding ransomware affiliates [S4]. MDCOA is use of stolen VPN sessions to enter a defense network and hand access to a ransomware group during a crisis. Candidate indicators: runnerw.exe launching PowerShell, rogue .msc files and MUIPath changes, unexpected .ppkg or .msi installs, and lookalike VPN domains [S1][S2][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track CVE-2025-26633 patch status on mission-relevant Windows systems and watch for the indicators above [S2]. (2) Authorities: user-awareness and help-desk verification procedures are command-controlled mitigations; actor attribution beyond vendor reporting should not drive response decisions [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce phishing-resistant MFA, because the actor captures one-time codes and session cookies in real time [S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and the DIB CS program for contractors, and coordinate with help-desk and VPN owners on callback verification [S4].

provenance.importedSummary: Water Gamayun exploits the MSC EvilTwin zero-day vulnerability to compromise systems and exfiltrate data, utilizing custom payloads and advanced data exfiltration techniques. Their arsenal includes backdoors like SilentPrism and DarkWisp, as well as information stealers such as Stealc and Rhadamanthys. They employ delivery methods like provisioning malicious payloads through signed Microsoft Installer files and leveraging LOLBins to maintain persistence and control over infected systems. Comprehensive analysis of their command-and-control infrastructure reveals sophisticated evasion techniques and dynamic control capabilities.
